svg.title: China ecommerce teacher feedback text expanded
svg.text: China’s cross-border e-commerce growth and its links to global industry
SILKLINK FOUR · Tian Qin · Jiacheng Tao · Yikai Wang · Peitong Song

g.text: China’s e-commerce connects online shopping with international trade. Four views explain how trade has grown, how shoppers’ purchase origins
changed, why overseas markets differ and how wider services support an order.
TRADE
SHOPPERS
MARKETS
SERVICES
TRADE GROWTH IS LED BY EXPORTS
Cross-border e-commerce trade
China · 2018–2024 · RMB trillion
Exports
Imports
A slower growth rate still means expansion
Annual growth was uneven: 25.7% in 2020, 7.1% in 2022, 15.3% in 2023 and 14.0% in
2024. The total kept rising across these years, even when the growth rate slowed.
For firms, this distinction matters: slower growth is still expansion, but stock and
delivery plans may need to allow for different rates of change. [1]

svg.text: Exports account for most of the expansion

g.text: China’s cross-border e-commerce trade rose from RMB
1.06 trillion in 2018 to RMB 2.71 trillion in 2024, up
156.4%. Exports increased by 251.9%, against 25.0% for
imports. The gap means that the expansion was
concentrated in selling abroad. Imports also grew, so
their falling share should not be confused with an
absolute fall in purchases from overseas.
The trade mix links China’s growth to overseas customers
and the services needed to fulfil their orders. Our
interpretation is that firms should consider customer
acquisition, payments and delivery together when planning
export activity. A growing national total can provide
context for that planning, but it does not show demand
for an individual product. The figures establish which
trade component expanded; they do not isolate the
causes.
Source [1]: Ministry of Commerce (2025), Table 11, p. 62; China Customs data. Calculations use published values in RMB 100 million, before conversion to rounded trillion labels. Service
interpretation also draws on UNCTAD [5].
CHINA-ORIGIN PURCHASE SHARE REBOUNDS TO 37%
Origin of the latest cross-border purchase
Share of surveyed shoppers reporting China (%)
2016–2023: +11 percentage points
The overall increase hides a reversal
China’s share was 26% in 2016 and 37% in 2023, an 11-percentage-point increase.
However, the endpoint comparison hides a reversal: the share fell from 36% in 2019
to 30% in 2022, before rising by seven points. The 2023 result was only one point
above 2019. Sellers therefore have reason to examine the intervening years when
assessing demand, rather than extending a smooth upward trend. [2,3]
The percentage measures the reported origin of
surveyed frequent cross-border shoppers’ latest
purchase, rather than the value of all sales. The trend
uses 24 countries, while the full 2023 survey covers
32,510 shoppers in 41 countries. This distinction matters
when comparing the survey with China’s national trade
totals: the two sources describe different populations
and measures.
In the full survey, 71% were very or extremely satisfied
with the delivery location, compared with 42% for
customs, a 29-point gap. Our interpretation is that an
exporter could investigate how buyers receive customs
information and how delivery is coordinated. These are
practical questions to test in the intended destination;
the survey does not establish why satisfaction differs or
whether these services caused the purchase-origin trend.
Sources [2–3]: Fan / HKTDC (2024), slide 8; IPC (2024). Trend: 24 countries. Full 2023 survey: 32,510 frequent cross-border shoppers in 41 countries. All eight annual observations are
published values.
REGIONAL OPPORTUNITIES DIFFER
China and 11 RCEP partner markets
Allocated export proxy / model-implied exports
Japan

Laos
South Korea
Australia
Singapore
Malaysia
Indonesia

Categories use 2013–2022 country averages:
Below 0.8
More unused potential
Scope to develop
Above 1.2
New approaches needed

svg.text: Read the model before the colour

g.text: Each ratio compares an allocated export proxy with
model-implied exports. A lower value means less proxy
trade relative to the benchmark, not necessarily a
smaller market. Japan and New Zealand average 0.580
and 0.619; Thailand and the Philippines average 1.676 and
1.783. Below 0.8, the authors identify unused potential;
above 1.2, they suggest innovative trade models or new
trade areas.
New Zealand’s 2022 ratio is 0.83, above 0.8, although its
period average is below that threshold. A decade-wide
category can therefore hide later changes. Our
interpretation is that firms should compare both the
level and the time pattern, then investigate local demand,
payments and delivery. These historical model ratios can
help frame questions about a destination; they cannot
establish future sales or an effect of the RCEP
agreement.
Source [4]: Zhang and Asraf bin Abdullah (2026), Table 19. Groups use 2013–2022 averages. RCEP: Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership. Bilateral exports are allocated proxies,
not directly observed flows.
E-COMMERCE RELIES ON WIDER SUPPORT SERVICES
Business e-commerce in 43 economies
US$ trillion · includes domestic and B2B sales
reported rise
Reading the estimates carefully
Both years include estimated components. The 2022 business-sales total is indicative: about one third
of the total is estimated.
37 major online platforms · partial coverage
US$ transaction value · ≈55% rise reported by UNCTAD
Business e-commerce sales across 43 economies rose
from almost US$25 trillion in 2021 to an indicative
US$27 trillion in 2022. The separate 37-platform
compilation increased from around US$2.6 trillion in 2019
to US$4.0 trillion in 2021. These measures answer
different questions: the scale of business e-commerce
and the activity recorded by selected intermediaries.
They cover different periods and activities, so they
cannot be added.
Six platforms account for 80% of sales in the
37-platform compilation. UNCTAD also describes
payments, warehousing, delivery and analytics supplied by
platforms. Our interpretation is that these
intermediaries can help sellers reach customers while
creating dependence on a few providers. Read alongside
China’s export growth, the figures draw attention to
service partners involved in overseas selling. They do not
show that China caused the changes in either the
multi-economy business-sales total or the platform
compilation.
Source [5]: UNCTAD (2024), pp. 3–4 and 31–32. Rounded figures and source-reported growth rates. The 43-economy total includes domestic and B2B sales; 2022 is indicative. Platform
coverage is partial. CC BY 3.0 IGO.
THE SERVICES BEHIND AN ORDER
E-commerce is often seen through an app or a website, but a
physical order connects sellers, shoppers and several supporting
services. Stock must be available, payment has to be arranged, and
goods need to reach the buyer. UNCTAD describes platforms
offering warehousing, logistics and analytics as well as online
transactions. IPC’s survey also treats customs and delivery as parts
of the shopping experience. This service view helps explain why
China’s expanding cross-border trade is relevant to firms beyond
the shopfront. [3,5]
CONNECT DEMAND WITH FULFILMENT
Our interpretation is that an export opportunity involves both
finding customers and organising the services around the order. For
example, a seller considering another destination could compare
demand evidence with the payment and delivery options available
there. The trade chart gives the national scale, the shopper survey
shows reported purchase origins and satisfaction, and the regional
model highlights differences worth investigating. Using them
together helps frame a business question without treating them as
interchangeable proof of demand. [1–5]
These photographs illustrate services. They do not document particular Chinese
firms or prove a growth trend.
Stock and picking.
Delivery to the buyer.
Online payment.
Order processing.

g.text: Exports represented 79.5% of the 2024 total, up 21.6 percentage points since 2018. Imports accounted for 20.5%,
although their value also increased. The shift therefore reflects faster export growth. Our interpretation is that
overseas customers and order-fulfilment services deserve attention together when firms consider this changing trade
mix. Source [1].

g.text: Exports contributed RMB 1.54 trillion of the RMB 1.65 trillion net increase; imports contributed RMB 0.11 trillion. The
93.3% export contribution separates the source of the additional trade from the 79.5% export share of the final
total. One measures change, the other composition. Neither identifies the causes of growth. Source [1].

g.text: Thailand rose from 1.335 to 2.453; Japan changed from 0.653 to 0.690. The scatter compares ending levels and
changes since 2013, while the heatmap shows the intervening years. A high ending ratio and a large increase answer
different questions. The movement describes a proxy/model ratio, not a sales growth rate. Source [4].

China’s cross-border e-commerce trade expanded from 2018 to 2024 mainly through exports. Frequent shoppers in 24 trend countries reported a higher China-origin share of their latest cross-border purchases, while historical model ratios differed among 11 RCEP partners. Our interpretation is that overseas demand should be

considered alongside local market conditions and order fulfilment. Platforms, payments, logistics and analytics connect this activity with wider industry. Firms can use these comparisons to investigate customers and service quality, while keeping trade values, survey responses and model estimates distinct.
